CAPM
Flat SML

CAPM

ROLL (1977)
The true market spans unobservable bonds, real estate and human capital; equity-only CAPM tests are limited. This shifted research toward multifactor models.

content.text: The factor zoo is both a library and a warning. slides.title: The 2×3 Sort
bullets:
2×3 SORT
Independent sorts

SIZE
Split the universe into small and big by market capitalization; independently sort the chosen characteristic into low, middle and high buckets.

INTERSECT
Cross the two rankings to form six portfolios; compare high with low within each size group.

HML
HML averages the high-characteristic portfolios and subtracts the low-characteristic average across size buckets.

2×3 SORT
HML = ½(SmallHigh + BigHigh) − ½(SmallLow + BigLow). Higher characteristic returns minus lower, averaged across size.；A Fama-French-style 2×3 sort works as follows: split the universe into small / big by market cap, split the characteristic into low / mid / high by breakpoints, then form six portfolios. Independent sorting keeps the characteristic spread from merely proxying for firm size; the same template applies to profitability or investment.

Every subsequent factor tutorial (05 value, 06 momentum, 07 quality, 08 other) drills into one family; this one gives you the asset-pricing lineage, the taxonomy, the "why do factors earn premia" debate, and the sober statistical reality of the factor zoo — so that when you read a paper claiming a new anomaly with a t-stat of 2.1, you know exactly how skeptical to be. items.text: The crucial epistemic point: **"anomaly" is model-relative, not absolute.** A characteristic is an anomaly with respect to a specific benchmark model. As benchmark models expand (CAPM → FF3 → Carhart4 → FF5 → FF6), yesterday's anomaly becomes today's risk factor, and what remains "anomalous" shrinks. This is why the number of "factors in the literature" and the number of factors that survive against an *expanding* set of controls are very different numbers — a theme central to Section 5.

items.text: - **Flat/too-flat SML — the betting-against-beta puzzle.** Black, Jensen, and Scholes (1972) sorted stocks into beta-ranked portfolios and found that realized average returns were far less sensitive to beta than CAPM predicted — the empirical line was flatter than the theoretical SML, with low-beta stocks earning more, and high-beta stocks earning less, than CAPM implied. Frazzini and Pedersen (2014) later formalized *why* this happens: many real-world investors (pension funds, retail investors, mutual funds under mandate) face leverage constraints — they cannot borrow freely to lever up a low-beta portfolio to their desired risk level, so instead they overweight high-beta stocks directly as a leverage substitute. This constrained-investor demand bids up high-beta stocks (lowering their expected return) and leaves low-beta stocks relatively underbought (raising their expected return relative to CAPM) — producing exactly the flat SML observed empirically, and motivating a **Betting-Against-Beta (BAB)** factor that goes long leverage-adjusted low-beta stocks and short leverage-adjusted high-beta stocks. This is the empirical seed of what became the **low-volatility / betting-against-beta anomaly** (Tutorial 08).

items.text: **q-theory rationale (brief).** In a standard investment-based model, a firm invests until the marginal cost of investment equals marginal Q (the present value of the incremental cash flows the investment generates). Firms with high expected profitability (ROE) and low expected new investment (I/A) are, in equilibrium, firms whose discount rate (cost of capital, i.e., expected stock return) must be high enough that they choose *not* to invest more — this again derives value/profitability/investment premia from a no-arbitrage-plus-production-technology argument, structurally parallel to, but derived independently of, Fama-French's dividend-discount argument. That two very different theoretical routes (consumption-side present value vs. production-side investment theory) arrive at "profitability up, investment down $\Rightarrow$ higher expected return" is considered a meaningful cross-validation in the literature.

items.text: No serious practitioner needs a factor to belong purely to one camp. What matters is whether the story predicts when the factor should fail. Value can fail when distress risk is realized; momentum can crash at sharp rebounds; low volatility can suffer when leverage constraints relax; size can fail when the microcap premium becomes crowded or untradeable.

items.text: The factor zoo problem is simple: hundreds of published anomalies cannot all be independent sources of expected return. Some are aliases for the same latent exposure, some are subsumed by known factors, some are too expensive to trade, and some are false discoveries produced by multiple testing.

It should have an economic rationale, point-in-time construction, robustness across periods and universes, low correlation to existing factors, implementability net of costs, and a multiple-testing-aware validation record.

8. Styles of Factor Portfolio Construction | 因子组合构建方式
items.text: The same factor can be expressed several ways: long-short decile portfolios, rank-weighted dollar-neutral portfolios, long-only tilts versus a benchmark, residualized signals inside an optimizer, or factor-mimicking portfolios for risk models. A long-short academic factor tests a premium; a long-only index enhancement portfolio tests whether the signal improves benchmark-relative stock selection under constraints.

items.text: Factor timing is tempting and difficult. Valuation spreads, recent factor returns, macro regimes, volatility, and crowding indicators can all contain information, but they also add another layer of multiple testing. The safer default is not aggressive factor timing; it is diversification across factors with drawdown-aware risk budgeting.

items.text: A factor is not yet a strategy. A strategy needs universe rules, forecasts, portfolio construction, execution assumptions, risk limits, capacity estimates, monitoring, and governance. items.text:
- It is known at the time it is used.
- It has a reason to exist before seeing the backtest.
- It survives neutralization to obvious exposures.
- Its IC, portfolio sorts, and regression tests agree directionally.
- It works across reasonable horizons and universes.
- It is not just a renamed existing factor.
- It survives costs and turnover.
- It has a failure story and monitoring plan.

14. Summary | 小结
items.text: The factor zoo is both a library and a warning. It gives researchers a vocabulary for systematic return patterns, but it also shows how easily finite noisy data can produce beautiful false discoveries. Good factor research therefore combines theory, data discipline, conservative testing, cost realism, and humility about regimes.

items.text: 因子动物园既是资料库，也是警告。它为系统性收益模式提供语言，但也说明有限噪声数据多么容易产生漂亮的虚假发现。因此，好的因子研究必须结合理论、数据纪律、保守检验、成本现实，以及对市场状态的谦逊。
